prologue: Years Later • The World Tour Begins
The sound of cards being shuffled.
An improvised table on a beach near Barcelona. Four players. A small crowd gathering around them.
A cramped café in Paris. People stand outside, trying to look through the windows as a hand reaches its conclusion inside.
A dark nightclub in Berlin. Music pounding. Lights flashing. Somewhere in the back, partially hidden between the crowd — a card table.
CUT TO: A rooftop somewhere in South America.
CUT TO: A narrow side street in Tokyo.
CUT TO: A café somewhere in Africa.
CUT TO: An apartment in New York.
CUT TO: A tournament on a beach.
CUT TO: A packed hall with hundreds of spectators.
Newspaper headlines. Social-media posts. Homemade posters. Livestreams. Photos. More and more titles appear.
Then the same title appears again and again.
A long table. The Great Eight are together again. For the first time in quite a while.
SCHOLAR has a tablet in front of him, surrounded by notes, statistics, tournament results and printed articles.
JESTER holds up one of the posters.
Apparently this man is World Champion.
He drops it onto the table and picks up another.
I'm beginning to think the title has lost some exclusivity.
WILDCARD leans back in his chair.
Sharp looks at the collection of posters.
OPTIMIST scrolls through footage of crowded tables. People cheering. People playing in parks, bars and on beaches.
SCHOLAR swipes across his tablet. More tournaments appear. More cities. More countries.
CLOSER has not said anything yet.
SCHOLAR turns the tablet around. A world map appears. Dozens of names are scattered across it. Each one followed by the same word: CHAMPION.
The room goes quiet. Everyone looks at him.
CLOSER stands and walks toward the world map.
He looks at the map. Hundreds of little points of light.
It's too big now to pretend it'll organize itself.
JESTER slowly looks around the table.
JESTER looks at the pile of homemade World Champion posters.
Somewhere, three hundred self-declared world champions just felt a disturbance in the universe.
The world map expands. All six continents illuminate: Europe, Africa, Asia, North America, South America and Oceania.
OPTIMIST studies the scale of it.
We can't do all of this at once.
The map zooms in. Europe fills the screen. Ten locations begin to glow. No names yet. Just ten points.
Population density. Travel infrastructure. Established playing scenes. Multiple distinct cultures within relatively short distances.

open: Rome. Warm evening. Scooters, ancient stone, crowds and terraces. A local man asks CLOSER something in Italian. CLOSER answers naturally without slowing down.
No, no, no. You speak Italian?
I have discussed considerably less relevant things with you.
Later, from a higher point overlooking the city, CLOSER points out routes, crowds and traffic patterns.
When you run forty-two kilometers through a city, you learn where people gather.
There. That's where we test this.
Ten tables. One champion. Then we find out whether this idea actually works.

1: You ran a marathon through this city and you're worried about nine tables?
I think that's the first time the marathon has made less sense after the explanation.
2: Twenty-seven minutes after the first table.
If that number doubles again, we need barriers.
3: Better now than at the World Championship.
4: People who had been watching are now playing their own games.
5: The Great Eight sit at a small restaurant. Food covers the table.
Halfway. I propose we formally recognize Italian food as part of the ruleset.
Scholar turns the tablet. Closer's eyebrow moves.
6: A handmade GREAT EIGHT — WORLD TOUR banner now hangs over the crowd.
Our branding department is going to be furious.
7: The future Italian Champion wins at a nearby table. He does not celebrate loudly.
I don't trust people who don't celebrate.
8: Excellent. I've been preparing for television for years.
Who gets to call themselves Champion?
That's what we're here to build.
10: I thought winning Rome meant I was ready.
It means you earned the chance to become ready.
You really do have a gift for congratulations.
What Sharp means is that you played well.
You made us work for it. That is enough for today.
Closer produces the first World Championship envelope.
You didn't need to beat us. You already beat Rome.
You represent Italy. We will see you at the World Championship.
You can make absolutely anything sound depressing.
ITALY COMPLETE — WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP 1 / 60 SEATS FILLED
The group stands around the Europe map.
You don't know what I was going to ask.
You're going to ask whether I've run another marathon somewhere.
That is not how marathons work.
Optimist stares at Madrid on the map.
I really do not like it when one of you says that anymore.

open: Warm afternoon light. Madrid is busy, loud and alive: terraces, music, football shirts and people talking over one another. OPTIMIST walks slightly ahead of the group without checking a map.
He has also changed clothes: a light linen shirt, tailored trousers and loafers. Nothing theatrical, but unmistakably more Madrid than what he wore in Rome.
Closer turns up in Rome looking suspiciously Italian, and now you arrive in Madrid dressed like you own half the terraces.
I am calling it now. Every city, one of you is going to start dressing like the place.
I do not know yet. But I am going to enjoy finding out.
They continue. OPTIMIST turns left, crosses a square, takes another street and greets a shopkeeper in Spanish. The shopkeeper replies. OPTIMIST answers naturally and keeps walking.
No, no, no. You speak Spanish too?
You lived in Madrid for a year?
Apparently we are not very good at talking about ourselves.
One runs marathons through Rome. One secretly lived in Madrid. Would anyone else like to confess to owning a castle before we continue?
CHARMER slowly raises one finger. JESTER immediately points at him.
Come on. I know where we start.
Plaza Mayor is full of terraces, spectators and improvised Dame de Pique tables. Four official tournament tables sit among the crowd.
This was always one of the busiest places.
PLAYER clears the first Plaza Mayor table.

11: More challengers are joining every few minutes.
12: A loud Spanish argument breaks out beside the next table.
They are deciding where to eat.
13: No single player is separating from the field yet.
It means the selection is competitive.
Madrid always liked making things difficult.
You talk about this city like an ex-girlfriend.
Everyone looks at OPTIMIST. He is already walking toward the next table.
We are coming back to that.
14: Closer, do not even think the word marathon.
The Great Eight move through side streets. OPTIMIST points out old favourites as they go.
Best coffee I found was there.
That place stays open far too late.
How much of that wardrobe did you already own?
Oh, this is definitely becoming a thing.
MADRID LOCATION TWO — EL RETIRO / PALACIO DE CRISTAL
The second tournament cluster sits around El Retiro near the Crystal Palace. The space is greener and calmer, but the players are more patient and serious. Five public tables remain.
This is where the stronger games usually ended up.
Thank you for translating reality into numbers.
15: At a nearby terrace, food arrives. OPTIMIST has ordered for everyone without asking.
Did you ask anyone what they wanted?
Fine. You may continue controlling Madrid.
I think this is the first time we have stopped moving since Rome.
16: A young local player loses badly, then immediately sits at another practice table.
That. Lose. Learn something. Sit down again.
17: A charismatic Spanish contender wins again. The crowd clearly knows him, and he knows they are watching.
Then he will have to prove the second part.
18: The contender approaches the Great Eight after another win.
PLAYER clears Level 19. At the same time, the Spanish contender wins the public Madrid tournament.
19: You won Madrid. Enjoy it. You earned it.
CLOSER gives the Champion a smaller card: a location and a time, not the World Championship invitation.
MADRID KEEPER'S TABLE — PRIVATE ROOFTOP OVERLOOKING GRAN VÍA
Night. Madrid glows below. One private card table waits high above the city. No crowd, no tournament noise. The Spanish Champion arrives and looks around.
You already proved you can win with everyone watching.
PLAYER + CLOSER + OPTIMIST vs SPANISH CHAMPION + TWO LOCAL PLAYERS
20: Madrid chose you. Spain chose you. Now you represent them.
The Spanish Champion takes the World Championship envelope. He is disappointed by the loss, but already energized by the rematch.
Next time, I am not losing.
Later, the Europe map returns. Portugal begins to glow. SHARP looks at it a little too long.
That was not suspicious at all.
SPAIN COMPLETE • WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP — 2 / 60 • PORTUGAL AVAILABLE

open: Morning. Porto: the Douro, steep streets, blue-and-white tiles and the Luís I Bridge. SHARP arrives in dark trousers, white shirt, fitted navy jacket and a subtle patterned scarf.
We are here to play cards.
The first four public tables line the Ribeira waterfront. SHARP studies the bridge above them, puts his bag down, reaches up to a safe training bar near the viewpoint and starts doing pull-ups.
We have been here eleven minutes.
You two should never be allowed to own the same stopwatch.
We are sightseeing. Normal people take photographs.
SHARP drops down, picks up his bag and looks at the tables.
That bridge counts as gym equipment now. For you specifically.

21: You have such a gift with people.
22: I could get used to this.
Average decision time is lower than Madrid.
There is a famous river directly behind you.
23: A waiter passes carrying glasses of port. SHARP follows the tray with his eyes for half a second. JESTER catches it.
24: You know where we are going?
They cross the Luís I Bridge on foot. SHARP looks upward at the structure.
Look at him. Scarf. Scenic route. Secret opinions.
PORTO LOCATION TWO — JARDIM DO MORRO
Five public tables sit above the river near Jardim do Morro. The atmosphere is younger, louder and more competitive.
25: Drinks arrive. Water, coffee, soft drinks — and one glass of port placed directly in front of SHARP.
You wake up before sunrise to train.
You just did pull-ups by a bridge.
SHARP tastes the port, pauses and looks at the glass.
You identified the age from one taste.
How long has this been a thing?
The human training schedule drinks fortified wine.
You corrected me. We are never letting this go.
26: A focused Portuguese contender begins to separate from the field. He clearly dislikes losing individual hands even when he wins the match.
27: The contender wins again, then immediately studies a mistake from the previous hand.
He is angry and he won.
Maybe he thinks he should have won better.
This version of Sharp is unsettling.
28: PLAYER clears Level 29. The Portuguese contender wins the final public tournament round. He is proud, relieved and already annoyed by every mistake he made on the way there.
29: CLOSER hands over the Keeper's Table card. The Champion reads: a historic port lodge in Vila Nova de Gaia.
PORTO KEEPER'S TABLE — HISTORIC PORT LODGE, VILA NOVA DE GAIA
Night. Rows of barrels disappear into the cellar. Porto glows across the Douro through tall windows. A glass of port sits beside SHARP.
You won Porto. Now you play us.
You already earned the invitation. This tells you where the level is.
PLAYER + CLOSER + SHARP vs PORTUGUESE CHAMPION + TWO LOCAL PLAYERS
30: CLOSER places the World Championship invitation on the table.
To us. You did not lose Portugal.
Then remember that feeling. You have until the World Championship.
Good. Next time I will not make that mistake.
You learned the words ten minutes ago.
The Netherlands begins to glow on the Europe map.
PORTUGAL COMPLETE • WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP — 3 / 60 • NETHERLANDS AVAILABLE

open: Rotterdam: modern skyline, trams, river traffic and the Erasmus Bridge in the distance. CHARMER arrives in clean trousers, minimalist jacket, fresh sneakers and one small orange detail.
Italian Closer. Spanish Optimist. Portuguese Sharp. Dutch Charmer.
I saw it. I liked it.
Four public tournament tables sit beside the Markthal and Binnenrotte. The crowd is busy, direct and close to the action.
Oh, this is going to be excellent.
You see why I like Rotterdam.
Because people tell you the truth?

31: Good game. Your middle hand was terrible.
Good game. Terrible hand. Both can be true.
32: The Dutch woman watches CHARMER smile through a conversation.
You know you smile too much?
33: The Dutch woman wins at another nearby table.
Normally people let me pretend longer.
34: They walk toward the Erasmus Bridge. SHARP looks upward.
You look at bridges and see gym equipment.
ROTTERDAM LOCATION TWO — ERASMUS BRIDGE / WILHELMINAPIER
Five more public tables line the modern waterfront near the Erasmus Bridge and Wilhelminapier. The Dutch woman arrives with the contenders.
You could pretend to be happy to see me.
35: I am talking about the cards.
37: Then why use the rest of the sentence?
38: I win it, I am champion.
You really do smile too much.
PLAYER clears Level 39. The Dutch contender wins the final public match and accepts the applause with a simple smile and handshake.
39: CLOSER hands over the Keeper's Table card.
Are all conversations here six seconds long?
ROTTERDAM KEEPER'S TABLE — EUROMAST AT NIGHT
Rotterdam glows below the private table high above the city. PLAYER, CLOSER and CHARMER face the Dutch Champion and two local players.
You really know how to make a man feel special.
40: CLOSER places the invitation on the table.
Right. Good. Because I want another game.
And next time I do not plan on losing.
Someone willing to tell me the truth.
London begins to glow. JESTER looks at PLAYER, then at London, then back at PLAYER.

open: London: black cabs, red buses, the Thames, old stone beside glass towers. PLAYER has adopted a sharper understated London look. JESTER immediately notices.
We are five countries in. You know exactly what.
A passer-by recognizes PLAYER. Then another. Then several people ask for photos while the others are barely noticed.
You did not tell us you were famous.
Another fan walks straight past the others and calls PLAYER by name.
Apparently some of us are more famous.
Four official tables sit amid Covent Garden crowds and street performers. Spectators gather around PLAYER before the first match even begins.

41: Well played. Rather inconvenient having half of London cheer against you, though.
Do not apologize. I would have enjoyed it too.
42: PLAYER, are the Great Eight here to choose Britain's World Championship representative?
We are here to find them.
The reporter moves on. PLAYER notices the others smiling.
43: A young player asks PLAYER what they missed. PLAYER takes the time to explain.
You did not have to do that.
Look at him. Beloved and educational.
44: The Great Eight finally escape the densest part of the crowd. WILDCARD looks back at the fans still waiting for PLAYER.
PLAYER's recognition rate has increased significantly since the World Tour started.
They are not recognising him because he is louder than us.
They watched what happened before the Tour.
They saw him bring us together.
You were already the Great Eight.
JESTER smiles, deliberately breaking the seriousness.
Which is unfortunate, because your ego is going to become unbearable.
He is literally the least likely one here.
Why is everyone looking at me?
Five public tables sit along the Thames near the South Bank and London Eye. The crowds are larger, the media thicker, and PLAYER merchandise has started appearing.
Why would you tell him that?
45: A calm British contender wins nearby, then takes a cup of tea before the next round.
One should not abandon civilization merely because there is a tournament.
46: Confident would be a touch premature. Cautiously optimistic.
47: PLAYER gets away from another group of fans. The British contender waits politely.
You appear to have acquired quite the following.
Rather inconvenient for the rest of us. I was hoping you would be exhausted by the time we met.
Did he just threaten you with manners?
It is supposed to be about all of us.
It is. They are just using you to tell the story.
48: Try not to sign too many things before then.
PLAYER clears Level 49. The British contender wins London, shakes his opponent's hand before celebrating and accepts the crowd with understated satisfaction.
49: Thank you. I must admit, I was rather hoping we would arrive at this point.
CLOSER gives him the Keeper's Table card. He reads it, raises an eyebrow and folds it.
Well. You have certainly chosen somewhere with atmosphere.
LONDON KEEPER'S TABLE — PRIVATE LONDON EYE CAPSULE
Night. A private London Eye capsule has been prepared with one card table. The doors close and the wheel begins to climb. London slowly opens beneath them.
Good heavens. You do know how to arrange a card game.
And you have finally managed to escape your admirers.
Then we ought to make the most of the peace.
PLAYER looks out over London. CLOSER joins him before the match begins.
They are starting to treat me like I did this.
That is the point. You never tried to replace any of us. You gave us a reason to stay. People remember that.
The final hands play as the capsule approaches the highest point of the rotation. The Great Eight win near the top, with London beneath them.
50: Very gracious of you. Although “good” is not quite the word I would have chosen for my final few hands.
Quite. Unfortunately, “quite close” has never been a particularly useful victory condition.
CLOSER slides the World Championship invitation across the table.
You won London. This does not change that.
Then I am sincerely honoured. When we meet again, I intend to be considerably less accommodating.
The Champion adjusts his cuff, then looks at PLAYER one last time.
One final observation. You really ought to learn to decline the occasional photograph. Fame is terribly demanding.
The capsule reaches ground level. Cameras immediately turn toward PLAYER again. PLAYER looks at the other seven. They simply nod and move together into the crowd.

handoff: The Europe map returns. CLOSER asks the question that now ends every chapter.
WILDCARD is already looking at Brussels.
Oh no. We have seen that face before.
There are stronger tournament indicators elsewhere.
Three languages. Different regions. Different cultures. Different opinions about almost everything. And somehow it works.
Good food. Good beer. People who take cards far too seriously. And I know where to look.

open: Brussels: cobbled streets, old façades, trams and multilingual signs. WILDCARD walks ahead wearing a subtle black-yellow-red detail.
Which, coming from you, is worrying.
A local calls to WILDCARD in French. He answers. Another speaks Dutch. He switches. A tourist asks in English. WILDCARD answers that too.
No. Absolutely not. How many languages are you going to casually reveal today?
Your French is considerably better than I expected.
The problem is that every country one of you reveals another entire skill set.
My entire personality is asking questions.
Four public tournament tables sit among the guildhalls and crowds of Grand-Place. WILDCARD looks completely at home.
How exactly did you know there would be card tables here?

51: Two local players switch languages twice during the same discussion.
Did they just switch languages halfway through an argument?
You cannot keep using the country as an explanation.
52: PLAYER is surrounded by fans again.
53: WILDCARD returns with food for everyone.
Fine. Do not look that pleased with yourself.
As they walk, WILDCARD starts another fact.
You do not even know what I was going to say.
Does not matter. Facts are my thing.
54: The group heads toward the Atomium. WILDCARD keeps advertising Belgium.
You are a tourism office with legs.
Five public tables are staged around the Atomium, with reflective spheres and steel structures creating a completely different visual from Grand-Place.
This is where we find the winner.
55: A Belgian contender makes an unusual tactical switch and wins.
Of course you would like that.
Great. There are two of him now.
56: You know what you are looking for?
Do not worry. We are figuring it out as we go.
57: The contender watches another wave of fans surround PLAYER.
Did not say you were not.
He is right, though. We do not mind.
Speak for yourself. I mind a little.
A fan runs up and calls for JESTER. He immediately brightens.
58: I was not going to give a percentage.
One more win guarantees first place.
Then I suppose I should win.
PLAYER clears Level 59. The Belgian contender wins the final public tournament match, celebrates openly with friends and changes language mid-celebration.
59: They are all stealing each other's lines.
CLOSER hands over the Keeper's Table card. The Champion reads the address and grins.
BRUSSELS KEEPER'S TABLE — GRAND BELGIAN BEER HALL
Night. A huge traditional Belgian beer hall: wood, brick, old beer signs, bottle collections and rows upon rows of taps. Hundreds of people crowd around one central card table.
You could not find somewhere quieter?
I could. I did not want to.
How many beers do they have?
I like not knowing what is going to happen.
PLAYER + CLOSER + WILDCARD vs BELGIAN CHAMPION + TWO LOCAL PLAYERS
60: CLOSER places the invitation on the table.
You lost this table. You won everything before it.
Then next time, I am finishing the job.
After the formal match, the beer hall becomes a celebration. JESTER takes a sip of a beer WILDCARD chose for him.
I WILL THROW THIS AT YOU.
WILDCARD stands near the doorway with PLAYER and looks back at the mixed crowd.
Everything is a little complicated. Languages. People. Everything mixed together. Still works.

handoff: The Great Eight step outside into the cool Brussels night. A distant nightclub bass line leaks down the street.
SCHOLAR stops. His head turns. Another beat drops.
That was absolutely an excited woof.
No. You knew what that was.
You do not get to make a happy woof and walk away.
SCHOLAR glances once more toward the club, then gives up.
I know where we should go next.
BELGIUM COMPLETE • WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP — 6 / 60 • GERMANY AVAILABLE

open: Early evening. Berlin: concrete, old stone, graffiti and trains overhead. SCHOLAR arrives in black trousers, black shirt, black jacket and black shoes.
Would now be a good time to discuss the other things?
Excellent. What are the other things?
We are here to find Germany's best player.
You look like you are about to decide whether the rest of us are allowed into a nightclub.
He is doing the clothes thing.
Four official tournament tables sit among historic buildings around Museum Island and the Spree.
This is the Berlin I expected you to know. Museums. History. Architecture.
Nothing. I am waiting for the weird part.

61: Third hand. That was where I lost it.
62: Is that what we are calling it?
63: A nearby musician starts playing electronic music. SCHOLAR's foot taps once. He stops it immediately. JESTER sees everything.
64: Does the route happen to pass any nightclubs?
On the way they pass a club entrance. SCHOLAR glances at the queue.
YOU KNOW WHEN THE QUEUE STARTS?
BERLIN LOCATION TWO — EAST SIDE GALLERY / SPREE
Five tournament tables sit by the East Side Gallery and river. The atmosphere is younger, louder and more experimental.
65: A German contender wins, then immediately writes notes instead of celebrating.
He won. Why does he look disappointed?
He is not disappointed. He is finding the parts that could have been better.
66: Heavy bass starts somewhere nearby. SCHOLAR turns instinctively.
It is a good sound system.
67: The group stops for food. The questions finally corner SCHOLAR.
How many Berlin clubs do you know?
OH, THIS IS SO MUCH WORSE THAN I THOUGHT.
How often have you been here?
You are the most structured person here. But apparently you used to disappear into clubs until Sunday.
That is precisely why I am structured now.
I was not always like this. There was a period when I did almost everything on impulse.
That might be the most disturbing thing you have ever said.
68: If I win, I finish first.
Then there is nothing else to discuss.
PLAYER clears Level 69. The German contender wins the tournament, checks the standings, closes his notebook and allows himself one small smile.
69: CLOSER hands over the Keeper's Table card. The Champion reads it, then looks directly at SCHOLAR.
BERLIN KEEPER'S TABLE — UNDERGROUND INDUSTRIAL TECHNO CLUB
Night. Concrete, steel, darkness, lights and bass. On a private industrial mezzanine above the main floor, one Dame de Pique table waits. SCHOLAR looks completely at home.
Interesting environment for someone who prefers control.
Control is useful because environments are not.
PLAYER + CLOSER + SCHOLAR vs GERMAN CHAMPION + TWO LOCAL PLAYERS
70: You lost. You are not upset?
Of course. But being upset does not alter hand six.
The others look at SCHOLAR, who is visibly pleased.
CLOSER slides over the World Championship invitation.
Then I need to improve before the World Championship.
At the World Championship, hand six does not happen.
Then I will need a different opening.
I appreciate people who learn before they react.
A new track begins below. SCHOLAR recognizes it. JESTER sees the expression.
SCHOLAR takes off his jacket and heads toward the stairs.

handoff: Much later. Early morning. Everyone looks exhausted except SCHOLAR, who is somehow composed again.
Because six hours ago you were a completely different person.
He is going to keep saying that now.
The Europe map appears. WARSAW, COPENHAGEN and PARIS remain. SCHOLAR deliberately steps back. JESTER is unexpectedly quiet, staring at Warsaw.
Because I want to see it.
Destroyed. Rebuilt. Changed. Still there. I started reading about it a while ago.
Your animal facts are not useless either.
Thank you. Finally someone with culture.
Mine. You had Belgium. Poland is mine.

open: Warsaw. Reconstructed old streets meet a modern skyline. JESTER is unusually attentive, already looking at buildings instead of trying to make everyone laugh.
JESTER points at a historic detail and gives a surprisingly accurate fact. SCHOLAR turns toward him.
Eastern Europe has history and animals. I contain multitudes.
WARSAW LOCATION ONE — CASTLE SQUARE / OLD TOWN
Four public tournament tables sit around Castle Square and the reconstructed Old Town. The setting gives JESTER endless material.
This is exactly why I wanted to come.
That is not what synergy means.

71: You actually watched the whole table.
I just usually make that harder to notice.
72: Do not say it like that.
73: So Poland understood the assignment before we arrived.
74: CASTLE SQUARE / OLD TOWN COMPLETE • WARSAW — 4 / 10
A local round of drinks loosens the group as they move toward the second location.
WARSAW LOCATION TWO — ROYAL ŁAZIENKI PARK
Five public tables sit around Royal Łazienki Park, with water, palace architecture and greenery. The mood is calmer, but the tournament is tightening.
And one history fact about the Palace on the Isle.
75: The group sits together after the match. JESTER has somehow chosen the venue and the drinks.
I have no idea what you are talking about.
And look how well everyone is getting along.
76: A Polish contender makes a strange, fearless play and wins. A friend hands him a small vodka. He toasts, drinks, then immediately sits for another match.
77: The contender wins again and gets another toast. He is visibly more relaxed and more creative.
Is he drinking after every win?
That should not be how graphs work.
78: Another drink. Another decisive victory. The Great Eight are now genuinely impressed by this specific player's ability to stay sharp while loosening up.
He is getting harder to beat.
PLAYER clears Level 79. The Polish contender wins the national selection with a bottle in hand, friends around him and noticeably more confidence than when the day began.
79: One drink, I relax. Two drinks, I see game better.
CLOSER hands him the Keeper's Table card. He reads: Palace of Culture and Science, 30th floor.
WARSAW KEEPER'S TABLE — PALACE OF CULTURE AND SCIENCE, 30TH FLOOR
Night. A private table sits high over Warsaw. The Polish Champion arrives carrying the same bottle. The Great Eight can see the city stretching beneath them.
PLAYER + CLOSER + JESTER vs POLISH CHAMPION + TWO LOCAL PLAYERS
80: You played your best match tonight.
Somehow you got better every time you drank.
CLOSER slides over the World Championship invitation.

handoff: The Europe map appears. Only COPENHAGEN and PARIS remain. CLOSER asks whether anyone has a preference. Nobody really does.
Without assigning heads or tails, SHARP immediately pulls out a coin and flips it. He catches it, looks down and announces the result.
Heads for what, you absolute genius?
The result contains no decision-making value.
We just flipped a coin to discover that the coin has a head.
WILDCARD looks at Paris, then smiles.
Ten countries. Ten champions. We finish Europe there.
And I have always wanted to go to the Moulin Rouge.
There it is. The actual reason.
We finish the continent. We celebrate. We have some well-deserved downtime.
Your definition of planning remains concerning.
For the record, heads was Copenhagen.
YOU DID NOT KNOW THAT FIVE SECONDS AGO.

open: Copenhagen. Water, bicycles, clean lines and calm streets. Nobody has a secret connection to the city this time. For the first time, the chapter belongs to the group rather than one individual.
Denmark has a smaller population than several of our previous stops, but organised card participation is unusually dense.
PLAYER is recognized by a group of fans almost immediately. They are respectful but clearly excited.
Nine countries in and somehow you are still getting more famous.
Can we not make that a thing?
Four public tournament tables sit along colourful Nyhavn beside the canal, cafés and boats. The setting is relaxed; the card play is not.
Colourful houses, water, cards. Very civilized.
You literally did pull-ups next to a bridge.

81: You three know people can simply say they enjoyed something?
82: A local player politely dismantles an opponent, then calmly resets the cards.
Not everything efficient belongs to Germany.
Look at Scholar defending regional nuance.
83: SHARP and SCHOLAR disagree about an early contender.
Let them argue. It is educational.
Neither of them is changing their mind.
84: The Great Eight move through central Copenhagen toward City Hall Square. A wave of bicycles forces everyone aside.
I have survived Queens, vaults, two-table trials and Berlin nightlife.
Copenhagen traffic may be how I die.
Stay out of the bicycle lane.
That advice would have been useful three seconds earlier.
SHARP looks at the city hall steps.
Do not turn Denmark into cardio.
COPENHAGEN LOCATION TWO — CITY HALL SQUARE / TIVOLI EDGE
Five public tables occupy the busy square beside City Hall, with Tivoli lights beginning to glow as evening falls. The tournament crowd is denser and noticeably serious.
85: A calm Danish contender begins to emerge. He plays with understated confidence and speaks only when necessary.
And people like playing against him.
86: The Danish contender wins, then spends time helping the player he just beat understand a difficult hand.
SCHOLAR discreetly makes a note. Nobody asks what the note is for.
87: People enjoy the table even when he beats them.
88: Do you always analyze people this openly?
Only when they are standing right there.
PLAYER clears Level 89. The Danish contender wins the national selection. He accepts congratulations calmly, shakes hands and gives the crowd a restrained smile.
89: And people actually enjoy sitting with you.
